World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Chinese company launches legal action over forced sale of Port of Darwin
World.content:
The Chinese-owned company which owns Darwin port has launched international legal action to try and stop the federal government from stripping it of the strategically sensitive asset.

It says the government's move is "discriminatory" and breaks Australia's obligations under its free trade pact with Beijing.

Anthony Albanese pledged at the federal election that Labor would return the port to Australian hands, saying it was necessary for national security.

The government has since been locked in negotiations with Landbridge as it tries to secure an Australian buyer and has flagged that it is willing to force the company to hand over the port if necessary.

But last month the owner of Landbridge, Ye Cheng, lodged a case with the World Bank's International Centre for Settlement of Investor Disputes requesting "arbitration proceedings".

It is the first time a case has been brought against Australia at the international tribunal, according to trade publication Global Arbitration Review.

Treasurer who leased Darwin Port would do it again Former NT treasurer Dave Tollner describes the federal government's plans to take back the 99-year lease of Darwin Port as "an appalling waste of money".

In a statement, Lanbridge said the actions by the federal government were "discriminatory and inconsistent with Australia's obligations under ChAFTA".

"Landbridge acquired its interest in the port through a fair, open and competitive process in full compliance with all applicable Australian laws and regulatory approvals," it said.

"Multiple Australian government reviews have confirmed there are no national security concerns.

"Having engaged with the Commonwealth in an effort to reach a constructive resolution, Landbridge has regrettably been unable to achieve a satisfactory outcome through dialogue alone and is now taking the necessary steps to protect its legal rights."

Transport and Infrastructure Minister Catherine King said the government was 'disappointed' by this decision. (ABC Ballarat: Coco Veldkamp)

In a statement the Transport and Infrastructure Minister Catherine King said the government was "disappointed by this decision" and would "defend the claim in accordance with established processes".

"The government has been in good faith discussions with Landbridge to reach a mutually acceptable deal to return the Port of Darwin to Australian ownership for several months," Ms King said.

"We intend to continue these discussions."

As recently as November last year, Ms King said the ongoing negotiations with Landbridge were "constructive".

The legal action could make it difficult for the government to deliver on its promise on Darwin Port within this term of government, with legal experts warning that international legal action at the tribunal can stretch on for years.

James Paterson says the government should "force a sale without any further delay". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Coalition has also pledged to return Darwin Port to Australian hands, and the Shadow Defence Minster James Paterson said the government should not "cave in" to Landbridge's "tactics".

"The Port of Darwin must be returned to Australia's sovereign control — as the Prime Minister promised it would during the election," Senator Paterson said.

"If the operator won't sell on reasonable commercial terms, the Commonwealth should use the powers available to them under the constitution to force a sale without any further delay."

Ms King said the government "remains committed to returning the Port of Darwin to Australian hands".

"We have been conducting discussions in a respectful and private manner and do not think it is in either party's interest to carry the dispute out in the public domain," she said.

Associate professor Colin Hawes from the University of Technology Sydney, who specialises in Chinese corporate governance, said a dispute in the ICSID could take years to resolve.

He said the tribunal has been used by an increasing number of Chinese-owned companies, where they have been blocked from global markets on national security grounds.

"It is being used in the United Kingdom, Sweden, Denmark, I believe," he said.

"Various Chinese companies that have been excluded from markets based on national security reasons have challenged those decisions, using this dispute forum.

"So in that sense, it's not unusual for a Chinese company to go through that body."

The ABC has also contacted Mallesons — the law firm representing Ye Cheng — and requested comment.

World.title: May temperature records fall across Victoria as warm weather continues
World.content:
Weather records have fallen like dominoes across Victoria today, as a spell of summer-like conditions continued into the first day of May.

West of the city, Avalon and Geelong were the warmest places in the state, with unseasonably high top temperatures of 29.3 degrees Celsius, tying for top spot with Walpeup, in the state's north-west.

Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist Dean Narramore said the Avalon and Geelong top temperatures were among a string of May records set across Victoria, in places as far afield as Nhill, Horsham, Portland, Colac, Bendigo, Morwell, Shepparton and Aireys Inlet.

"Looking at very preliminary numbers, there were probably at least 20 locations that have seen their warmest May day on record across the state," Mr Narramore said.

"And interestingly, because we're going to see these warm, northerly winds continue tonight … we actually could see a number of locations also have their warmest May night on record as well, particularly through western and south-western Victoria."

Aireys Inlet, on Victoria's Great Ocean Road, hit a summery 28.7 degrees Celsius. (ABC News: Nicole Mills)

Mr Narramore said the high temperatures were more like those usually expected in February or March, and about 10 to 14C above average for this time of year.

"Even around Melbourne itself, a number of locations have seen their warmest May day on record, including Melbourne Airport at 27.1, Essendon at 27 and Moorabbin at 28.1," he said.

He said the unusually balmy weather was caused by a high-pressure system hanging around the Tasman Sea, which had been directing northerly winds across Victoria.

"But today and tonight, we've seen a cold front, a really strong cold front, move into South Australia," he said.

"That's strengthened those northerly winds and dragged that warm air even further south today."

Another warm day at Seaford Beach, south-east of the city. (Supplied: Melinda Saunders)

Sadly, for lovers of shorts and T-shirts, the summer-like conditions will soon come to a screeching halt.

"We've got this big, strong, cold front moving into Western Australia and South Australia today and tonight that'll sweep across Victoria Saturday night and Sunday, with a band of rain, strong and gusty winds, and many areas will drop 5 to 10 degrees," Mr Narramore said.

So, be prepared to dig out your usual autumn attire from Sunday onwards, including your umbrella.

"This is it. Get out today, tonight, tomorrow. That's it after that," Mr Narramore said.

Some of the May records broken today

World.title: Community 'disappointed' by Sheraton high-rise approval
World.content:
Lobby groups against a seaside Sheraton high-rise resort say they have mixed feelings about the development going ahead with a reduced height that still exceeds the planning scheme.

In 2024 the Fraser Coast Regional Council approved Sunny Beach Land's application to build an 18-storey, five-star Sheraton Resort at Hervey Bay, three hours north of Brisbane.

Revised plans reduce the two 18-storey towers approved by council. (Facebook)

It would have been the largest hotel development north of Brisbane but the local branch of the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland (WPSQ) appealed the decision, on the grounds that light emanating from the building would impact on endangered sea turtles and migratory birds.

It said the 18-storey development should be reduced to six storeys, the maximum height allowed in the area under the council's planning scheme.

After 19 months of mediation meetings between the developer, WPSQ and the council, revised plans were lodged with the Planning and Environment Court on Thursday.

Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland lodged the appeal to protect endangered sea turtles and migratory shorebirds from the impacts of the resort's lighting. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

In the documents, the developer agreed to lower the height of the building's residential tower to 16 storeys and the hotel tower to 12 storeys.

The basement car park has been removed to address noise concerns, and exterior lighting has been reduced.

On Friday the Fraser Coast Regional Council confirmed in a statement that the court had approved the development and resolved the appeal.

Celebrity Jamie Durie took part in the developer's pitch to council. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

WPSQ Fraser Coast branch president John Williams said the group was satisfied by the compromise which avoided further costly legal action.

"Wildlife was hoping to reduce the building height to something nearer the six-storey limit provided for in the planning scheme," he said.

"However, we realise that there are risks and costs in litigation. Accordingly, we thought it was prudent to settle at a point where we believe we had made significant gains against the 18 storeys that council had approved.

"There were also negotiated changes to the conditions to ensure that the fragile marine environment was better protected."

Community activist Sue Brooks says she felt mixed emotions at the resolution of the long-running appeal. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Sue Brooks is a former local councillor and the leader of the Torquay Towers Appeal Group which funded the appeal.

She said she felt mixed emotions at the resolution of the long-running appeal.

"There's disappointment that one of the buildings will still be 16 storeys high, we have not got a building in Hervey Bay to that height," she said.

"But there's also relief that this is now completed because we're into year two. For a lot of us, it's consumed a lot of work and emotional input."

While she accepted that all avenues for appeal have been exhausted, Ms Brooks held out hope that escalating construction costs would make the project unviable.

"I'm still hoping that this building isn't constructed, I think economic conditions will be the deciding factor as to whether there is money to go ahead and construct it," she said.

The appeal's supporters are concerned the development's approval will set a precedent for more high-rise development along the Hervey Bay seashore. (Supplied: Sunny Beach Land Pty Ltd)

In a statement Sunny Beach Land director Dan Cuda welcomed the outcome.

"A vast majority of the local community support this project and understand its value as a catalyst for continued growth and a prosperous future for Hervey Bay," Mr Cuda said.

"Today's decision is an exciting result that will see the creation of a world-class, five-star hotel and residential development, putting the Fraser Coast on the map as global tourism destination."

The development's lighting design will reduce the building's impact on sea turtles by minimising artificial skyglow, he said.

Councillor Paul Truscott was one of six councillors to have approved the development, with five against.

In a statement, Cr Truscott noted that the development would still include a five-star hotel, residential apartments and recreational facilities.

"This means the project will still deliver the same core uses approved by council in 2024," he said.

World.title: Former teacher jailed for grooming teenage boy
World.content:
A woman who groomed and sexually abused a teenage boy while she was working as a high school teacher near Newcastle has been sentenced to at least two years in prison.

Karly Rae, 37, pleaded guilty to four offences, including having sexual intercourse with a child aged between 14 and 16, grooming a child for unlawful sexual activity and possessing child abuse material.

The Newcastle District Court heard Rae was working at a Hunter high school when she contacted her 15-year-old victim via social media in September 2024.

The boy attended the same school, but did not know Rae because she worked on a different part of the school campus.

Judge Peter Marr today sentenced Rae to a maximum three years and three months' jail, with a non-parole period of two years.

"I'm satisfied no sentence other than imprisonment can be the only sentence in relation to this matter," he said.

Rae cried and tried to speak to the judge as the sentence was handed down.

Someone sitting in the public gallery yelled out "don't do this, please".

The court was told the pair communicated several times before Rae asked the boy to join an encrypted app.

She suggested they should hang out, and later took him to a local sportsground, where she had sexual intercourse with him.

Several days later, Rae admitted in messages to her victim that she "should never have done it".

She told her victim "it's my fault" and "I take full responsibility".

Karly Rae pleaded guilty to several offences, including grooming a child for sexual activity. (Supplied: Facebook)

When Rae was arrested, police took her phone and found messages she sent on social media to the boy that included several videos where she exposed herself.

Rae also admitted to committing an act with the intention of perverting the course of justice.

The court heard that while she was on bail, with an apprehended violence order in place, Rae called the victim and asked him to lie.

No positive school memories: victim

The court heard the victim struggled to think of positive memories from his time at school.

A victim impact statement was read out to the court on his behalf.

"Every time I drive past the school I think about it," the statement said.

He said that now he understood what happened to him, he cried.

The statement said every time he heard the word "schoolteacher", he thought about what happened to him.

The victim said he felt like he had let his family down.

Judge not convinced about remorse

Judge Marr took several factors into account when handing down the sentence, including moral culpability, remorse and the risk of reoffending.

He said he did not think Rae would reoffend in this way.

The court heard that leading up to and at the time of Rae's offending she was experiencing mania, resulting in increased energy, increased sex drive and an impairment in judgement.

Judge Marr said he was satisfied the expert report was accurate.

But he told the court he was yet to be persuaded that genuine remorse had been exhibited by the offender.

Karly Rae cried when she was handed a prison sentence in Newcastle District Court. (ABC Newcastle: Robert Virtue)

The court heard she had admitted what she did was wrong and felt embarrassed.

But Judge Marr said she had failed to put herself in the shoes of a 15-year-old.

He noted she met the victim at her place of work, a school, and had recently completed a course on her responsibilities to child protection.

World.title: Tough-on-crime NT government snubs youth incarceration Senate inquiry
World.content:
Federal senators from across the political spectrum have criticised the Northern Territory government for snubbing a federal inquiry into youth justice and incarceration held in Darwin.

The Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee sat in Darwin for two days this week, hearing evidence from statutory officers, advocacy and legal groups and Indigenous organisations.

The Senate inquiry has previously held sessions in Melbourne, Perth and Sydney and is scheduled to submit its report at the end of June.

The Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee heard evidence in Darwin across two days. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

South Australian Liberal senator and committee chair Leah Blyth said when the inquiry held local hearings in other jurisdictions, applicable government departments had given evidence, but they had failed to show in the Northern Territory.

"It is disappointing that the Northern Territory [government] didn't get involved in this inquiry," she said.

"We certainly would welcome any kind of submission that they would like to make."

Leah Blyth is chairing the inquiry. (Facebook: Leah Blyth)

Greens senator David Shoebridge berated the NT government's absence.

"It's a bloody disgrace the NT government is not here," he said.

"If they were at all proud of their work, they'd turn up and defend it, and they're obviously not."

A tough-on-crime agenda

Since coming to government in 2024, the Country Liberal Party (CLP) government under Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro has implemented a series of tough-on-crime reforms affecting young people in the territory.

They include reducing the criminal age of responsibility from 12 to 10, removing detention as a last resort and reintroducing spit hoods to youth detention centres.

The CLP has pointed to victims of crime statistics from NT police for proof its policies have been effective. They show around 2,000 fewer reported victims in 2025 than in 2024.

Lia Finocchiaro says the CLP's policies have been effective at reducing crime. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Throughout the two days of hearings in Darwin, the inquiry heard testimony about the transfer of youth detainees from Alice Springs to Darwin.

The Office of the Children's Commissioner said relocations could have devastating impacts on the children themselves as well as close family.

"We've seen the closure of the Alice Springs Youth Detention Facility, resulting in the automatic transfer of detained Central Australian children to the one facility here in Darwin, 1,500 kilometres away from family, community and country," commissioner Shahleena Musk.

Shahleena Musk was the first person to give evidence at the inquiry's Darwin sitting. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Liberal, Labor and Greens senators each raised concerns about the relocation of children between custodial facilities, sometimes without their parents' knowledge.

"This would be a scandal if it was happening in Sydney or Melbourne or Brisbane," Senator Shoebridge said.

"It's hard to believe, really."

David Shoebridge says there should be more scrutiny over how Commonwealth money is spent by the NT government. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency (NAAJA) criminal youth lawyer Matilda Hunt said while police had a responsibility to try to contact the family of arrested youth, attempts were often short-lived and unsuccessful.

"One of the biggest aspects of our daily job at court is going through a list of fresh custodies to track down family," she said.

Federal funding of the NT in the spotlight

During the Darwin hearing, several participants also noted the NT was going backwards on seven of 19 Closing the Gap targets, including youth incarceration.

Responding to testimony from NAAJA lawyers, independent Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe questioned how Commonwealth money was being spent in the territory.

Around 80 per cent of the NT government's revenue comes from the federal government.

"Are we wasting our time even relying on any kind of relationship or any funding from the Northern Territory government, when the federal government can step in here and take control of this situation?" she said.

Lidia Thorpe criticised the NT government for not appearing. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Larrakia elder Eric Fejo urged the federal government to intervene in the NT's law and justice system for the benefit of Aboriginal Territorians.

"I think the federal government, if their hearts were really into it, they would do an intervention," he said.

" They've got the power, they can do it if they choose. "

Eric Fejo says the Commonwealth should intervene on youth justice issues in the NT. (Felicity James)

Senator Blyth said there had been calls from organisations to link Commonwealth funding to Closing the Gap targets in the NT.

"At the end of the day, this isn't the government's money, this is the people of Australia's money," Senator Blyth said.

" We've got to make sure that anything that we're doing, any projects, are actually getting the outcomes that are desired. "

Remote council jobs a priority in NT Aboriginal affairs plan The NT government has released its Aboriginal Affairs framework as the territory goes backwards on several Closing the Gap targets.

Senator Shoebridge said funding should flow directly to Aboriginal-controlled organisations, rather than through the NT government.

"Every time a young person is being put in shackles and flown from Alice to Darwin, 80 per cent of that is coming from the Commonwealth — that is not right," he said.

"80 per cent of their funding comes from the Commonwealth and then they thumb the nose at the Commonwealth when we want some answers."

The NT Department of Corrections said it was "committed to operating the NT's youth justice system in accordance with the established legal frameworks of the Northern Territory ".

"[The department] engages regularly with a broad range of stakeholders to support continual improvement across the system," a spokesperson said.

The NT Department of Education said it operated under NT legislation and regularly engaged with a range of stakeholders.

World.title: School traffic warden hit by delivery truck in regional WA
World.content:
A school traffic warden in his 80s is recovering in hospital after being hit by a truck at a busy intersection in WA's South West.

Emergency services were called to the corner of Paris Road and Barnes Avenue in Australind just after 7:30am today.

Police said the warden stepped out in front of a Woolworths delivery truck before being struck.

He suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, and was taken to Bunbury Hospital for treatment.

The truck driver stopped and is helping police with their inquiries.

Andy Elliott says the traffic warden was struck by a delivery truck. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

South West Police Acting Superintendent Andy Elliott said there was no suggestion alcohol or speed were factors in the incident.

He said there were multiple witnesses to the crash, possibly including children.

"People were conveying kids to school, there were cars around," Acting Superintendent Elliott said.

Warden recovering in hospital

Acting Superintendent Elliott said police at Australind were investigating and were speaking to the warden, who remained in hospital this afternoon.

"He is 80 plus," Acting Superintendent Elliott said.

" Sometimes age can be a factor in a week or so when unexpected things happen, so we're hoping for the best. "

Traffic wardens, who are employees of WA Police, have been calling for more support in the Australind area in recent months.

Several wardens resigned from their positions at Australind crossings in December due to escalating safety concerns.

Members described hazardous drivers and having beer bottles, cups of coffee and on one occasion, a knife thrown at them.

Traffic concerns from residents

Residents have been calling for improved safety at the intersection for several years, and say they are frustrated with the slow progress.

Local Belinda Williams said she frequently used the intersection and was horrified by Friday's incident.

"Absolutely devastating, I think my heart just hit the floor," she said.

"I think that it was going to happen. I'm devastated that it's happened to anybody.

"Everybody knows the crossing guard, everyone loves the crossing guard."

The incident happened at the corner of Paris Road and Barnes Avenue. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

Ms Williams said the crossing was on a major arterial road, busy with thousands of commuters during peak hours, and could be dangerous for pedestrians.

She said she wanted authorities to review traffic management and consider roundabouts, traffic lights and pedestrian crossings, having already raised her concerns with the local council.

"You've got three major intersections in a short space of road," she said.

"I've seen cars driving down the footpath on the left … people get very impatient."

In a statement, the Shire of Harvey said safety around crossings was a "top priority" for the council.

The traffic warden was struck while on duty at a busy Australind intersection. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

"We acknowledge community concerns regarding traffic conditions in this area, and want to reiterate that the shire has been actively advocating for improved traffic management solutions," a spokesperson said.

The shire has installed traffic counters at multiple locations along Paris Road and says the counters will inform the development of "appropriate traffic management measures".

World.title: Family of Tiwi Islands sistergirl calls for life sentence for man who killed her
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

The family of a beloved Tiwi Islands sistergirl who "had so much to live for" has pleaded with a court to impose a life sentence on the man who killed her.

Last week a Northern Territory Supreme Court jury found Andrew Mungatopi not guilty of murder, but guilty of manslaughter, following a week-long trial, after almost a day of deliberation.

Pauline Grant (centre) told the court she would never forgive Andrew Mungatopi. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

Sistergirl is a term used by some Indigenous people to describe a gender-diverse person who has a female spirit.

The court heard Mungatopi stabbed his niece, Lena — whose family asked that she be referred to by her first name only — in the chest after an argument erupted at a family gathering in October 2024.

During sentencing submissions today, Lena's sister Pauline Grant read aloud her victim impact statement in court, describing her as someone with "the biggest heart".

Addressing Mungatopi directly, Ms Grant said her family would never forgive him for taking Lena's life and asked for the "justice she deserved".

Lena's family is calling for Andrew Mungatopi to be handed the maximum sentence of life in prison. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"Andrew, for the last couple of weeks, my family has watched those fake tears run down your eyes, run down your face," she said.

"This last year has brought so much pain where my mother and siblings find it hard to sleep, waking up most mornings crying in tears.

"I want you to know my mother, Agnes, and the family, would like you to get the full penalty — the maximum.

"You took a life."

Uncle 'worried', 'scared' after fatally stabbing sistergirl, court hears The partner of a man charged with the stabbing murder of a Tiwi Islands sistergirl tells the NT Supreme Court she saw him run outside "like a flash" before crying and repeatedly calling out "call the police".

In a separate victim impact statement also read to the court, Mungatopi's sister, Marlees Mungatopi, said she was traumatised by Lena's death and felt "ashamed to call Andrew my little brother".

"Lena was a beautiful, loving, caring and supportive person and what happened to [her] should never have happened," he said.

"Lena did a lot for our family, especially for Andrew and his family."

Ms Mungatopi also called for her brother to be sentenced to the maximum penalty of life in prison.

"He took a beautiful life [and] does not deserve to come out of prison," she said.

'An incredibly substantial knife'

In her sentencing submissions, Crown prosecutor Rhiannon McGlinn argued that when Mungatopi stabbed Lena with "a large kitchen knife", he was aware of a substantial and unjustifiable risk that he would kill her.

She said Mungatopi had escalated a confrontation when he slapped Lena across the face and then went inside and armed himself with what was "plainly, an incredibly substantial knife".

Lena's mother Agnes Lorenzo attended court during the trial and was visibly emotional after today's hearing. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

Ms McGlinn said Lena meanwhile went outside and picked up a milk crate.

"A milk crate, unlike a knife, is not automatically a dangerous or offensive weapon," she said.

" And she picked that milk crate up, the Crown says, to protect herself. "

Ms McGlinn argued that stabbing Lena with moderate force — after explicitly threatening to do so — led to the "inevitable conclusion" that Mungatopi understood his actions would cause a substantial risk of death.

Lena, a sistergirl from the Tiwi Islands, died after being stabbed in the chest by her uncle Andrew Mungatopi in 2024. (Supplied)

"He was told by people present to desist and he chose not to," she said.

"We do say Your Honour can be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the associated mental element for this manslaughter is of recklessness."

In the Northern Territory, manslaughter is defined as either reckless or negligent conduct causing death, with recklessness generally considered more serious than negligence.

While acknowledging the life maximum, Justice John Burns noted that maximum penalties should be reserved for cases which fall within the "worst category of that offending".

Ms McGlinn conceded the Crown was not submitting this was a worst case scenario, but maintained it represented a "serious example" of reckless manslaughter — compounded by Mungatopi's history of violence toward women and his absence of remorse.

Signs of remorse, rehabilitation

In his submission, defence barrister Ambrith Abayasekara argued that crucially, the jury had found that not only had Mungatopi not intended to kill Lena, but he had not intended to cause her serious harm.

"That's critical here because someone who doesn't intend to cause serious harm in that context, it's difficult to see how you can find beyond reasonable doubt that he was aware of the substantial risk of death occurring in those circumstances," he said.

Ambrith Abayasekara said his client's offending was below the mid-range of seriousness for manslaughter. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

Mr Abayasekara characterised the stabbing as a "two-sided" confrontation "where there was various upping the ante and a lot of posturing without anyone considering the consequences".

He said the offending fell below the mid-range of seriousness.

Mr Abayasekara also pointed to what he described as genuine indicators of remorse and rehabilitation, telling the court Mungatopi had indicated a willingness to plead guilty to manslaughter at the earliest opportunity.

The unit block in Malak where Lena was stabbed on October 8, 2024. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We also point to the factual matters of his immediate reaction at the time of the offending," he said.

" Shock, sadness, his attempts to save the life of the deceased, his distress, his calls for his own punishment at that time, as can be heard in the Triple Zero call. "

Mungatopi is expected to return to court for sentencing next month.

World.title: Bulldogs attack misfires again as Cowboys run riot
World.content:
It was only three weeks ago that Canterbury stood up and made the rest of the NRL take notice, knocking off competition leaders Penrith.

It certainly seems a lot longer ago than that.

The Bulldogs’ season is in danger of slipping away from them after a third straight loss, a 28-12 defeat against the in-form North Queensland Cowboys at Accor Stadium.

Scott Drinkwater and Reed Mahoney celebrate a try. Getty Images

The result gave the discarded Reed Mahoney the last laugh over his former team and leaves Cameron Ciraldo and his side continuing to search for answers.

The match was a dogfight until the Cowboys broke clear late on but Canterbury’s shortcomings in attack again came back to bite them.

Lachlan Galvin scored one of their only two tries, throwing a dummy to dash over the line for the fourth time in five starts.

Loading

The blame couldn’t be cast on him more than anyone else on Friday night but while the Bulldogs are turning in underwhelming performances like this, questions about whether he is a halfback will go on.

The last time these two sets of players had been in such close proximity was inside a Las Vegas resort nightclub in early March, when Mahoney and Bulldogs singer Marcelo Montoya reportedly traded verbal barbs.

Back then Canterbury were being cast as title contenders while Todd Payten was being positioned as the first NRL coach to lose his job this year after dropping their opening game to Newcastle at Allegiant Stadium.

How the tables have turned since then. The Cowboys are still holding out on a new deal for Payten but after six wins in seven outings now his case is becoming compelling.

The Bulldogs, meanwhile, are sliding further off the pace.

Losses against depleted Parramatta and Brisbane teams were deflating and this left a similar feeling for supporters, who began to stream out of the Olympic stadium in the final minutes of the game as two late tries sealed the deal for the Cowboys.

The Bulldogs were not short on toughness but lacked potency and imagination with the ball, failing to take opportunities to put their stamp on proceedings after drawing level when Josh Curran latched onto the spoils of a high kick from Galvin at the 53-minute mark.

The match was still in the balance until Cowboys centre Tom Chester burst into space with 14 minutes left, finding St George Illawarra-bound fullback Scott Drinkwater on his inside to cross for the second try of the night.

Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater. Getty Images

Canterbury captain Stephen Crichton attempted to rally his side but to no avail.

It was a fitting way for veteran Jason Taumalolo to mark equalling Jonathan Thurston as North Queensland’s most capped player.

The only downside for the Cowboys was another shoulder injury which cut short the evening of forward Jeremiah Nanai.

He had returned to action only a week earlier after recovering from an operation to the same shoulder in the off-season.

Nanai’s latest injury shapes as a blow for Queensland in the upcoming State of Origin series.

Canterbury have big problems of their own.

World.title: The Demons are playing bold and fast. Their CEO did the same, for just seven months
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 The Demons are playing bold and fast. Their CEO did the same, for just seven months Danny Russell May 1, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Not long into Paul Guerra’s tenure as Melbourne Football Club chief executive, it became clear he was going to do things differently. Unbothered by the reputation of Melbourne supporters for cheeseboards and wine, he promised a louder, jazzier match-day experience for home games at the MCG, with activated LED screens behind the players’ race and songs chosen by players after goals. Paul Guerra pressing the flesh in his short-lived sting at Demons CEO. AFL Photos via Getty Images “If I look at other sports like basketball, it’s kind of two hours of entertainment whiplash,” Guerra told this masthead in March. “Everyone is engaged. There’s never a dull moment.” On the field, the Demons were playing an attractive, high-octane style of footy under new coach Steven King. Most importantly, they were winning games, and sitting in the top four after seven rounds.



But behind the scenes, we now know, the relationship between Guerra – the former Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive – and his board had fractured. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Guerra was appointed last April. It didn’t take long for the Demons to get buyer’s remorse When Melbourne president Steven Smith fronted the media on Wednesday, the day after Guerra’s sacking shocked the football industry, he said there was a “general lack of confidence in his ability to lead the club, and a breakdown of relationship with the board”. “Basically, there was no one particular thing,” Smith said. It has become clear in the days since his dismissal that there were a number of different things that contributed to the decision.



Guerra was left “puzzled” and blindsided by his axing after seven months in the job, which has left him seeking legal advice. While he came to the job with political connections and a strong network of contacts in the racing industry, a Demons insider not authorised to speak publicly said any suggestion that Guerra was sacked because of his inability to secure a new $100m training base at Caulfield was wrong. Loading “When he took the job the whole process of Caulfield was already underway. [Vice-president] Geoff Porz was running the whole thing from the board,” the insider said. Porz took over the brief, reporting to president Smith and fellow board members, after the departure of CEO Gary Pert in October 2024. Guerra started in the role in September last year.



Guerra did sit in on some meetings involving the Demons, the Caulfield Racecourse Reserve Trust and Melbourne Racing Club, which runs Caulfield Racecourse. But the MRC did not blame Guerra for losing faith in the Melbourne Football Club project. An MRC source, who was not authorised to speak publicly, said the racing club objected to the Demons’ plans – building their headquarters on the southern side of the racecourse, Neerim Rd, which would require digging a tunnel under the track. The MRC source said building the tunnel would stop racing at the venue for 12 months – a scenario unacceptable to the racing industry.



They said the racing club offered up an alternative – building the football club’s home base on the northern side of the course, Station St, which has an existing tunnel – that was rejected by the Demons. “Paul comes into the role as CEO and is told ‘we as a board are running everything to do with Caulfield, it has been going for well before you even walked in the door, and we will look after that. You get on with the job of running the footy club – get us a coach, drive members’ engagement,” the club insider said. Melbourne president Steven Smith and interim CEO Brian Cook speak to the media on Wednesday, the day after Paul Guerra’s departure. Joe Armao They added that Porz had been seeking advice on Caulfield from external consultants FMRS – former advisers to premier Dan Andrews. FMRS is not a registered lobby group and is unable to make approaches or representations to state government officials on Melbourne’s behalf.





“His remit was Plan B. And Plan B was Waverley. But the board had no time for Plan B.” The AFL will determine the next tenant at Waverley Park after buying the training base from Hawthorn Football Club. Loading Richmond was one possibility. The Tigers need to vacate Punt Rd in September for eight months while their home base undergoes redevelopment. But Guerra was exploring Waverley as a 10-year option – a temporary base until the Demons secured a long-term home.



While there’s no suggestion Guerra’s plan to revolutionise the Melbourne match-day experience was a factor, this masthead has reported there was unease within the club before he even started in the role about his media-facing leadership style, accustomed as he was to public lobbying with VECCI. Another apparent misstep was reported by NewsCorp on Friday – that Guerra had upset members of the Demons board over a decision to invite Sam Stynes to a president’s function for Jim Stynes Day, an event honouring her late husband. The Stynes family at the MCG for Jim Stynes Day, honouring the late Melbourne legend, who won a Brownlow Medal and later became president of the club. Getty Images The Demons source confirmed Sam Stynes’ name was not on the original guest list for the day when Melbourne played Brisbane at the MCG in round 6 (Sunday, April 19). Years after the passing of Jim Stynes, Sam Stynes married to Demons vice-president Porz. They tied the knot in 2015, but have since split. Melbourne declined to comment on the report.



Smith told a press conference on Wednesday the board identified Guerra’s successor, Stan executive Dan Taylor, two weeks before sacking him – about the time Guerra sent out the Jim Stynes Day guest list. Nine Entertainment Co, owner of this masthead, also owns Stan. Veteran administrator Brian Cook will act as interim CEO until Taylor can start. View post on X After the Brisbane game, Guerra took the unique step of posting behind-the-scenes footage of Melbourne’s coaching staff on his LinkedIn profile. “The debrief… one of the most important moments for leaders and their teams,” the post said, revealing images of coach Steven King in conversation with other Melbourne officials.



“It would be easy to get carried away with the emotion. And you can see the lucky group of fans that experience the change room excitement. It’s a great place to be after a win. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Demons approached new CEO weeks before Guerra sacking “But in a room adjoining, the debrief has started. That moment that looks at what just happened… good and otherwise ... and the transition to what is needed for the next game and what we will bring. It sets the tone for the week ahead. “Whilst one of the background signs reads ‘Ruthless’, one of our team mantras, the pictures scream ‘Humble’. Ruthless in the determination for success and humble to do the basics to keep learning and getting set for the next challenge. “It all comes together in the debrief.”

The Dockers can fight their way back into this game, and might want to start by tagging Bont.

World.title: Jefferson Lewis could face life in prison. Traditional law calls for a different kind of justice
World.content:
NationalKumanjayi Little Baby case Jefferson Lewis could face life in prison. Traditional law calls for a different kind of justice Riley Walter May 1, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images of a deceased Indigenous person. After police found the body of Kumanjayi Little Baby on the banks of the Todd River, they vowed to bring to justice the man they say killed her. On the fifth day of a manhunt to find Jefferson Lewis, accused of abducting and murdering the five-year-old girl, Lewis surrendered to Charles Creek Camp. There, five kilometres from Kumanjayi Little Baby’s home, he was severely beaten by a vigilante group. Loading Unconscious, Lewis was handcuffed, bringing an end to a pursuit that had gripped the country. Still, the community wanted more. Hundreds rioted outside Alice Springs Hospital demanding payback; justice, they said, had not been done. As police cars were set on fire and rubber bullets were fired into an angry crowd, the community demanded that Lewis be handed over.



In the Indigenous communities of the vast central Australian desert, unwritten rules govern the way of life. Customary law, a deeply spiritual and swiftly enforced values system, often overrules the common law system of wider Australian society in Indigenous communities. In those ancient cultures, offenders must pay with an eye for an eye. Punishment, often referred to as “payback”, varies according to the crime committed and the cultural background of the offender. In the most extreme instances, some crimes can be punishable by death; men have faced traditional spearing, even after serving a prison sentence. But rather than a form of revenge, traditional payback is considered essential to peacemaking and preventing further violence; within communities, it is seen as a necessity to right wrongs. Kumanjayi Little Baby and Jefferson Lewis. In some instances, offenders have evaded police until they have received the traditional punishment owed them under customary law. So deeply ingrained in communities is the enforcement of customary – or traditional – law that Northern Territory courts have historically considered aspects of the values when sentencing offenders. Related Article Kumanjayi Little Baby case Jefferson Lewis was beaten before his arrest. This is how the riot began



The family of Kumanjayi Walker, a 19-year-old Warlpiri and Luritja man shot and killed by Northern Territory police constable Zachary Rolfe in 2019, said the officer should have faced traditional payback over the teenager’s death. Rolfe was acquitted at trial of Walker’s murder. An inquest into Walker’s death was told the payback – a spearing – would help the community of Yuendumu heal. The chaos that ensued on Thursday night, however, is not regarded by authorities and legal experts in the Northern Territory as an example of traditional punishment. What unfolded, they say, was rioting and violence. “We don’t accept that concept. There is one law and that applies equally to everybody,” Northern Territory Police Commissioner Martin Dole told ABC Radio on Friday morning. “I understand that there is an absolute sense of grief and loss, but can I be very clear? This behaviour cannot be excused, explained away or tolerated, and those responsible for doing that should be held accountable just as Mr Lewis is being held accountable.”



Lewis was flown to Darwin for medical treatment amid concerns for his safety if the crowd reached him. It is expected he will be charged at the weekend. Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family, too, called for calm amid the chaos. “This man has been caught, thanks to community action, and we must now let justice take its course while we take the time to mourn Kumanjayi Little Baby and support our family,” her grandfather, Robin Granites, said. Lewis, despite the grief and anger that spilled onto Alice Springs’ streets, is now in the hands of the territory’s justice system. “Mr Lewis is in police custody. There will be a prosecution commenced, and the court case will proceed,” Dole said.



“That needs to be accepted by the community.” For cultural reasons, the name of the five-year-old victim will no longer be published, in accordance with the family’s wishes. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

A Queensland paramedic has been cautioned after he was found to have delayed leaving for jobs to get food and items from his house, including waiting for his McDonald’s to arrive before responding to potentially life-threatening call-outs.

On that occasion in May 2023, Luke William Hastings delayed leaving for a job by three to five minutes waiting for coffee and food at McDonald’s.

Hastings was cautioned for delaying leaving for jobs. Sam Mooy

During another incident in July 2023, he swung by his house to pick something up on the way to a potentially life-threatening event, causing a delay of 10 to 15-minutes.

World.title: Radical shake-up needed of rental market
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Radical shake-up needed of rental market May 1, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Come on Boomers, like, this is just so uncool. As a Boomer myself, and one with absolutely no desire to own multiple rental properties (or any other properties for that matter), I am ashamed and embarrassed by the article ″⁣How Boomer landlords control the rental market″⁣ (1/5). What happened to Flower Power, the Summer of Love, the counter-culture or helping your fellow human beings? It’s all gone out the window. The greed on display is disgraceful. If investment is your thing why choose real estate? Especially rental real estate. Unfortunately, here in Australia we don’t ″⁣do″⁣ compassion very well.

Many European countries have substantial amounts of rental housing but from what I believe it isn’t so cut-throat and there is a greater degree of stability and rental security provided for tenants. There is a house in our neighbourhood where the tenants are replaced every year and the rent goes up. This is no way to treat people.

It’s time for a radical shake-up of the rental industry.

David Legat, South Morang How to bring fairness into play

The best way to make the capital gains tax discount fairer is to extend the non-discount period from one year to six years, with no grandfathering. So the 50 per cent CGT discount would only apply if a property is held for six years, not one. This would only negatively impact property flippers, who buy, update, and sell properties after a year for the 50 per cent discount, and who outbid first home buyers at auctions. More properties would become available for younger buyers.

Importantly also, long-term investors would not be affected, so there would be no damaging property sell-off. Rental property availability and rent levels would therefore not be compromised. And with no grandfathering, the government would reap the increased tax revenues from day one.

Stuart McArthur, Carlton North Albanese is afraid of offending anyone

The decision by the Albanese government to move slowly on removing negative gearing on investment houses and the likely refusal to lower capital gains taxes on the sale of such houses is hardly surprising, if very disappointing. This is consistent with a government led by a very timid prime minister who seems deeply fearful of offending anyone at the top level of the economic pile. It represents a short-term political view taking no account of the long-term needs of the country.

There can be no doubt now that this is a government that has taken the ground of a Turnbull-like Liberal Party, a party which has now moved much further to the right.

Greg Bailey, St Andrews



THE FORUM Trump’s legacy

Your correspondent (Letters, 1/5) states history will not be kind to Donald Trump. Trump is obsessed with leaving a legacy, attaching his name to various structures ranging from memorial buildings to a class of US Navy battleships.

Will those actions affect history when recalling Trump? Those who disparage him have good reason to apply a wide range of derogatory terms in describing him. MAGA supporters believe that he can do no wrong.

In 20 years, when he is not around, how will qualified historians describe him in considered judgments?

I suggest there will be few that are complimentary about his terms as president of the United States.

Bill Pimm, Mentone Smart comparison

Surely James Comey was comparing Donald Trump with Maxwell Smart (″⁣Ex-FBI chief charged with threatening life of Trump after posting photo of seashells″⁣, 30/4).

Stephen Davies, Carlton North Cry me a river of tears

Columnist Peter Hartcher cites former Australian Intelligence Chief Paul Dibb in describing Donald Trump’s Iran war as the most pointless war since the Crimean War of the 1850s. One of the events of that war was the infamous Charge of the Light Brigade led by Lord Cardigan, who rode slowly at the head of his brigade along a long valley with the enemy firing down on them. As men were shot, troops simply closed ranks and proceeded behind their leader. When he reached the end of the valley, Lord Cardigan was at a loss as to what to do next as there had been no clear objective for the march (remind you of anyone?).

Cardigan then led his remaining troops back down the “Valley of Death” exposing them again to the rifle fire of the enemy.

This is one of many examples of heartless incompetence and stupidity that marked the Crimean War and I was struck by the justice of Dibb’s comparison with what has unfolded in Trump’s Iran “excursion”.

The world faces economic chaos, the Strait of Hormuz has become a ransom point for the shipment of oil and the Iranians are far from defeated.

In this context, Donald Trump declares victory. It makes me want to cry.

Jane Garvey, Camberwell Specialist strategy

It’s great to hear that high specialist fees are the next target for Health Minister Mark Butler. This is more about the hospital fees they charge, and the move may well face a High Court challenge. It will take a long time to implement. But a government that insists on promoting private provision of public services like NDIS and aged care might do well to consider that other part of the private theory: competition. Within months this government could fund bulk billing specialist clinics in the community, doctors paid a salary just like public hospital doctors. It has already done similar with its Urgent Care Clinics. It could supply the states with dedicated funds to employ more salaried specialists in public hospitals. The very specialists would not be affected but many other specialists would either lower their fees to compete or do some salaried work in the clinics.

Dr Tim Woodruff, president, Doctors Reform Society, Richmond



Errors of youth

How many of us did something in our youth that we have since regretted? We’re well into our twenties before our brains have matured, so it’s easy to make mistakes when young.

If a citizen of another country breaks our laws we insist that their country of origin accept them back. Likewise, we need to accept back the women and their children currently trying to survive in the basic and unhygienic Roj camp on the Iraqi-Syrian border (″⁣ISIS-linked families’ plan halted as PM stands firm″⁣, 1/5).

Certainly, once they’re back, thoroughly investigate whether they pose a threat to our society and take the necessary precautions.

What the prime minister’s mother would have said is irrelevant.

Virginia Heller, St Kilda East The hanky defence

Hooray Michael Bachelard (Opinion, 1/5). A friend recently decried the use of hankies as being unhygienic. I’d like to remind her they’ve been in use for years and I don’t know that they have been the cause of widespread infections. Instead I’ll send her a hanky enclosed in copies of all of today’s hanky letters, and Bachelard’s article. Besides, the design on the hanky that one buys says a lot about that person.

Margaret Collings, Anglesea No hankering for old days

My childhood experience of the hanky was a tad more traumatic than many Age letters correspondents.

In the 1960s when I went to school, the Grade 2 teacher at my Catholic primary school demanded each of her 64 students have a freshly ironed hanky on their desk at the start of the day.

Anyone who didn’t suffered a crack on the back of their hand with a blackboard ruler.

Sensible compassionate justice for a seven-your-old child don’t you think?

Brendan Douglas, Alphington Electric’s moment

Kevin Rudd is spot on in highlighting the crucial and precious opportunity to use the current threat to oil supply to pivot to our abundant affordable renewables (“Rudd hopes crisis drives green push”, 28/4).

Instead of spending billions on emergency oil supply and quid pro quo discount deals on gas exports we should be using those billions to help everyone go electric.

However, Rudd is also spot on when he uses the term “physical terror” to describe how terrified many mega-city suburban residents are in the face of the sudden petrol price rise.

On top of mega-mortgages, this is the tipping point for many people already on the brink.

Free public transport might be a popular gimmick in those suburbs served by trams and trains but what about the fringe? No wonder there’s drive-offs from servos.

Bernadette George, Mildura The nang scourge

The article about nitrous oxide canisters, commonly known as nangs, (‴⁣⁣Nang’ cylinders dumped across city despite health, environment risks″⁣, 28/4), is a good wake-up call to the waste problem they create, but only touched on the damage they inflict on young people.

These harmful canisters, supposedly for the catering industry, are packaged to appeal to teenagers and are available in milk bars and online, and can even be home delivered. They scramble the brains of children and lead them towards the belief that drugs are necessary to have an enjoyable time.

To remove this scourge, the Victorian government needs to look at recent legislation enacted in Western Australia where only registered catering businesses and cooking schools can obtain the canisters. We legislated to help stop inhaling from toxic paint canisters, now it’s time to act on the growing problem of these destructive nangs, which are just as damaging and accessible to children and teenagers.

John Nolan, Endeavour Hills



When a draw is a win

As a football supporter who equally dislikes both Hawthorn and Collingwood, the best possible result is a draw.

Peter Heffernan, Balaclava Changing partners

Now I understand – Melbourne did the boardroom equivalent of secretly finding a new partner before you flick the existing one.

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon Hand it to him

Not only is my hanky an insurance in case I sneeze or cut myself, it also keeps my keys and coins safely tucked into my pocket.

Peter O’Brien, Newport The war machine

You’d think that after WWII and its millions of deaths, its immense destruction and the sheer pain and suffering that wars bring, we would have resolved to never go to war again, but instead we made, and keep making, bigger, more powerful weapons in service to war. But not only that, as Warwick McFadyen recalls with Bob Dylan’s song Things Have Changed (Faith, 26/4) they have indeed. In the 1960s and ’70s we marched against war, whereas these days, it seems to me, that they are marching for more.

Henry Herzog, St Kilda East



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

With apologies to Kenny Rogers and his song The Gambler, Victoria is “on a train bound for nowhere”, (“PM ploughs billions into SRL despite inflation, war”, 1/5).

Ivan Glynn, Vermont Anthony Albanese’s provision of billions to prop up the dubious SRL rail project must be the most grotesque example of pork-barrelling to prop up a Labor mate in an election year.

Martin Newington, Aspendale



The “philanthropy” of Gina Rinehart in providing a plane for One Nation proves the adage that birds of a feather stick together.

Alan Inchley, Frankston I’m excited about Orangina Airways, but will it fly in a straight line or just continually turn hard right?

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick The hanky

No, Michael Bachelard (Opinion, 30/4). You are not singlehandedly bringing back the hanky. My daughter and I have been hanky users for many years. Beats having tissues in the washing machine.

Trish Young, Hampton Mum’s mantra to Dad as he left our house every morning of my ’50s childhood, “Keys, tobacco, money, handkerchief”.

Megan Peniston-Bird, Kew No need for a mobile phone memo-alert! Make a knot in your hanky corner!

Luise Mock, Tawonga South



Furthermore

Medical specialists have a captive market and they don’t like being called out, as Health Minister Mark Butler has done, for jacking up their fees to an excessive level (″⁣Doctors accuse Butler of playing ‘blame game’ over specialists’ fees″⁣, 1/5).

Phil Alexander, Eltham It is pleasing that the PM is going to implement the findings of the royal commission on antisemitism. Now, how about the Murphy report? Gambling destroys lives.

Christine Morris, Wyndham Vale Finally

Donald Trump wants interest rates to fall, but he’s doing his best to make them rise.

Malcolm McDonald, Burwood

World.title: AFL Friday night LIVE: Western Bulldogs’ chance for revenge against Freo under open Marvel roof
World.content:
You’ve got to hand it to the Western Bulldogs. They were expected to cop it from Freo tonight because of their debilitating injury list.

But the Bonts, sorry, I mean the Dogs, have been the better team in the first term. Once again their skipper has led from the front. Bontempelli amassed 15 possessions, playing a quarterback-type role.

Aaron Naughton has also been inspirational. Many feared for his future after a sickening crash landing last week, but here he is bouncing around like a first-year recruit. He has kicked two goals.

The other big inclusion has been the return of ruckman Tim English.

The Dogs have been slicker with their hands. They have had 28 more possessions than the lacklustre Dockers – 23 of them handballs. It has helped them jump to a 26-point lead

The Dockers can fight their way back into this game, and might want to start by tagging Bont.

World.title: Jefferson Lewis could face life in prison. Traditional law calls for a different kind of justice
World.content:
NationalKumanjayi Little Baby case Jefferson Lewis could face life in prison. Traditional law calls for a different kind of justice Riley Walter May 1, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images of a deceased Indigenous person. After police found the body of Kumanjayi Little Baby on the banks of the Todd River, they vowed to bring to justice the man they say killed her. On the fifth day of a manhunt to find Jefferson Lewis, accused of abducting and murdering the five-year-old girl, Lewis surrendered to Charles Creek Camp. There, five kilometres from Kumanjayi Little Baby’s home, he was severely beaten by a vigilante group. Loading Unconscious, Lewis was handcuffed, bringing an end to a pursuit that had gripped the country. Still, the community wanted more. Hundreds rioted outside Alice Springs Hospital demanding payback; justice, they said, had not been done. As police cars were set on fire and rubber bullets were fired into an angry crowd, the community demanded that Lewis be handed over.



In the Indigenous communities of the vast central Australian desert, unwritten rules govern the way of life. Customary law, a deeply spiritual and swiftly enforced values system, often overrules the common law system of wider Australian society in Indigenous communities. In those ancient cultures, offenders must pay with an eye for an eye. Punishment, often referred to as “payback”, varies according to the crime committed and the cultural background of the offender. In the most extreme instances, some crimes can be punishable by death; men have faced traditional spearing, even after serving a prison sentence. But rather than a form of revenge, traditional payback is considered essential to peacemaking and preventing further violence; within communities, it is seen as a necessity to right wrongs. Kumanjayi Little Baby and Jefferson Lewis. In some instances, offenders have evaded police until they have received the traditional punishment owed them under customary law. So deeply ingrained in communities is the enforcement of customary – or traditional – law that Northern Territory courts have historically considered aspects of the values when sentencing offenders. Related Article Kumanjayi Little Baby case Jefferson Lewis was beaten before his arrest. This is how the riot began



The family of Kumanjayi Walker, a 19-year-old Warlpiri and Luritja man shot and killed by Northern Territory police constable Zachary Rolfe in 2019, said the officer should have faced traditional payback over the teenager’s death. Rolfe was acquitted at trial of Walker’s murder. An inquest into Walker’s death was told the payback – a spearing – would help the community of Yuendumu heal. The chaos that ensued on Thursday night, however, is not regarded by authorities and legal experts in the Northern Territory as an example of traditional punishment. What unfolded, they say, was rioting and violence. “We don’t accept that concept. There is one law and that applies equally to everybody,” Northern Territory Police Commissioner Martin Dole told ABC Radio on Friday morning. “I understand that there is an absolute sense of grief and loss, but can I be very clear? This behaviour cannot be excused, explained away or tolerated, and those responsible for doing that should be held accountable just as Mr Lewis is being held accountable.”



Lewis was flown to Darwin for medical treatment amid concerns for his safety if the crowd reached him. It is expected he will be charged at the weekend. Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family, too, called for calm amid the chaos. “This man has been caught, thanks to community action, and we must now let justice take its course while we take the time to mourn Kumanjayi Little Baby and support our family,” her grandfather, Robin Granites, said. Lewis, despite the grief and anger that spilled onto Alice Springs’ streets, is now in the hands of the territory’s justice system. “Mr Lewis is in police custody. There will be a prosecution commenced, and the court case will proceed,” Dole said.



“That needs to be accepted by the community.” For cultural reasons, the name of the five-year-old victim will no longer be published, in accordance with the family’s wishes. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

A Queensland paramedic has been cautioned after he was found to have delayed leaving for jobs to get food and items from his house, including waiting for his McDonald’s to arrive before responding to potentially life-threatening call-outs.

On that occasion in May 2023, Luke William Hastings delayed leaving for a job by three to five minutes waiting for coffee and food at McDonald’s.

In a similar situation, also in May 2023, he waited roughly 15 minutes after being dispatched to depart, during which he ordered and waited for his coffee.

Hastings was cautioned for delaying leaving for jobs. Sam Mooy

During another incident in July 2023, he swung by his house to pick something up on the way to a potentially life-threatening event, causing a delay of 10 to 15-minutes.

World.title: Super Rugby Pacific: Hurricanes beat Crusaders to stay at top of table
World.content:
Photo: Masanori Udagawa/Photosport

Title credentials tested and passed.

The Hurricanes have keep their spot at the top of the Super Rugby Pacific ladder with a gritty 38-31 win over the defending champion Crusaders at home.

Wing Fehi Fineanganofo again crossed the chalk, as he looked to etch his name in competition history, while the Crusaders were unable to find a late strike to force extra time.

Leicester Fainga'anuku was again outstanding at flanker, kicking off the night's scoring with another powerful burst from close range, but after several kicking duels and an exchange of penalty goals, the 'Canes went bang-bang to demoralise the visitors before the break.

Halfback Cam Roigard played a hand in both strikes, setting one up for wing Josh Moorby, while finishing another, as the home side took a 24-10 lead at the break.

A try by halfback Noah Hotham offered hope for the visitors, as he sniped in from the base of a scrum, with a big dummy and sprint, but after hooker Raymond Tuputupu ran the perfect line off Roigard, the gate appeared to be shut.

The competition's leading tryscorer produced some more magic for his 15th of the season, moving to within one of Joe Roff and Ben Lam's record to give the hosts a buffer.

Then late drama, as flanker Dom Gardiner rumbled over, replays showing he lost the ball in scoring, but the points stood to set up a bumper finish in Wellington.

The Crusaders fired away for a late equaliser, but second-five David Havili ended his 150th appearance with the forgettable decision to kick the ball away and the Hurricanes hammered it into touch to bring curtains on a cracker in the capital.
